definition: Rectify means to correct something that is wrong — to act on an error, a fault, or an unfair situation until it is genuinely set right.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rectify. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rectify should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When the utility admitted it had overbilled four hundred customers, it promised to rectify the mistake before the next statement went out — refunds first, apologies second.
Patching is weaker than rectifying: a patch covers the fault so things limp along, while rectifying digs the fault out and sets the thing fully right.
An overhaul goes further than rectifying: rectifying fixes the specific wrong that was found, while an overhaul tears the whole system down and rebuilds it, sound parts included.

To correct is the everyday, all-purpose word for fixing anything from a typo to a bad habit. Rectify is its formal cousin: it is what officials, banks, and agencies do once a wrong has been identified and must be put right on the record.

To remedy is to supply a cure for a bad situation — the word looks toward relief, easing the harm the problem causes. Rectify acts on the fault itself: you rectify the billing error; you remedy the hardship it created.

Rectify means to correct something that is wrong — to act on an error, a fault, or an unfair situation until it is genuinely set right.

The registrar discovered that a scanning glitch had shaved a decimal point off dozens of GPA records, and she spent the week rectifying every affected transcript before colleges began requesting them.

Rectify is weightier than fix because it treats the mistake as a wrong that must be genuinely set right — the registrar is not tinkering with a machine but restoring each record to what it should have said all along.
Rectify is the formal word for putting a wrong right — an error, an oversight, an injustice — and it promises the fix is real, not cosmetic.
For everyday slips, fix or correct is plainer.

Two look-alikes to keep straight: "rectitude", moral uprightness, is a cousin from the same Latin rectus, but it names a quality a person has, while rectify names an action you take; and ratify, to formally approve an agreement, involves no fixing at all.

For weeks, patrons had hunted for titles the catalog swore were on shelves where they had never stood.
The head librarian refused the quick options -- a warning sign, a note on the website -- and ordered the staff to rectify the catalog itself.
